16. Longitudinal data: from events to analysis

David Sarrat González

Source: vignettes/book-16-longitudinal.Rmd
book-16-longitudinal.Rmd

What you will learn

Choose wide, long or person-period data; handle irregular measurements and missing periods; reshape privately; and fit a discrete-time hazard model and repeated-measure mixed models across two connections.

You need: the Opal login from Getting started, output formats and lab values. Run every section in order, including solutions. This chapter uses omop.gibleed, omop.synthea and the two Synthea sites. GiBleed and Synthea are public synthetic resources. Their results teach analysis mechanics, not clinical conclusions.

The same people, two shapes

Longitudinal means following the same people over time. A small invented example: three people measured on two days. Days are relative to each person’s entry.

Person Value on day 0 Value on day 30
A 14 15
B 13 NA
C 15 14

Turning the two measurement columns into rows gives this long picture:

Person Day Value
A 0 14
A 30 15
B 0 13
B 30 NA
C 0 15
C 30 14

This is a scheduled grid: B’s second row explicitly represents a missing value. An event-long table would omit B’s day-30 row if no event occurred. Its absence must not be interpreted as a measured zero. Six rows still represent three people.

Check. Which shape would you use to compare baseline means? Which for a model of change over time?

Worked answer

Use the wide day-0 column for baseline means. Use long data with a person key and time for repeated-measure models. Account for dependence between the same person’s rows. Taking an ordinary mean over long rows weights frequent attenders more.

Choose the shape before requesting it

Question Shape What a row means
Baseline lab or cross-sectional comparison wide One person or entry episode
How do repeated readings vary with time? long One observed measurement, with time since index
Did an outcome occur during this at-risk period? person_period One person-episode and time bin
How long until the first outcome or censoring? survival One follow-up record
When was an exposure active? intervals One exposure start and end

Time-varying covariates belong to periods: use information available by that period’s start. A future lab mean would leak future information into a hazard model. A survival output must specify censoring. Intervals retain both ends of an exposure; they are not automatically nonoverlapping. Chapter 8 executes all five shapes.

Start with GiBleed and request visit rows directly from a recipe.

library(dsOMOPClient)
conns <- ds.omop.login("https://localhost:8443", user = "administrator",
  password = "password", resource = "omop.gibleed", server = "site")$conns
visits <- omop_event("visit_occurrence", concepts = 9201L, name = "admission")
visitors <- omop_population("visitors", index = omop_index(visits))
visit_recipe <- omop_recipe(events = list(visits), populations = list(visitors),
  outputs = omop_output("visits", rows = "visitors", format = "long", sources = "admission",
    options = list(columns_derived = c("days_from_index", "duration_days"))))
recipe_execute(visit_recipe, out = c(visits = "D_visit_long"), datasources = conns)

The long table remains private. Release the setting counts to describe its rows.

visit_counts <- dsBaseClient::ds.table("D_visit_long$concept_id", datasources = conns)
visit_counts$output.list$TABLES.COMBINED_all.sources_counts
#> D_visit_long$concept_id
#> Inpatient_Visit              NA 
#>            1037               0

The table counts exactly 1,037 admission rows; chapter 4’s locator count was floored to the five-row band starting at 1,035. To count people separately, reduce each visitor’s records to a count and distinguish single from repeat visitors.

visits_per_person <- omop_study(visits, outputs = "baseline", baseline = list(
  admissions = omop_variable(event = visits, reducer = omop_reduce("count"))))
recipe_execute(visits_per_person, out = c(baseline = "D_visitors"), datasources = conns)
ds.omop.mutate("D_visitors", pattern = ifelse(admissions == 1,
  "One admission", "Repeated admissions"), newobj = "D_visit_patterns", datasources = conns)
dsBaseClient::ds.table("D_visit_patterns$pattern",
  datasources = conns)$output.list$TABLES.COMBINED_all.sources_counts
#> D_visit_patterns$pattern
#>       One admission Repeated admissions                  NA 
#>                 756                 134                   0

There are 890 visitors: 756 with one admission and 134 with repeated admissions. A long table does not guarantee repeated visits for every person. Inpatient Visit is concept 9201, found in chapter 4.

Summarise time since entry without fetching event rows.

Worked answer

visit_time <- dsBaseClient::ds.mean("D_visit_long$days_from_index", type = "combine", datasources = conns)
visit_time$Global.Mean
EstimatedMean Nmissing Nvalid Ntotal
studiesCombined 1272.55 0 1037 1037

The mean is about 1273 days: the first admission contributes zero, and subsequent admissions contribute positive offsets. Some people still have only one admission. This is an event-weighted mean, not the mean gap between admissions. Switch to Synthea for repeated numeric measurements.

Irregular measurements: define windows first 

ds.omop.disconnect(datasources = conns)
ds.omop.connect(resource = "omop.synthea", datasources = conns)
lab <- omop_event("measurement", concepts = 3000963L, value = "value_as_number",
  unit = omop_unit(8713L), name = "hb")
entry <- omop_population("entry", index = omop_index(lab))

Haemoglobin 3000963 and g/dL 8713 are the measurement and unit used in chapter 14. Index is each person’s first haemoglobin. These synthetic records are irregularly spaced over years. Use three 1000-day windows, not calendar years. Window 1 includes days 0–999, window 2 days 1000–1999, and window 3 days 2000–2999. First and last refer to actual dates within each window, not scheduled visits.

window_value <- function(which, start, end) {
  omop_variable(event = lab, reducer = omop_reduce(which,
    window = omop_window(start, end)))
}
windows <- omop_recipe(events = list(lab), populations = list(entry), variables = list(
  first1 = window_value("first_value", 0, 999),
  first2 = window_value("first_value", 1000, 1999),
  first3 = window_value("first_value", 2000, 2999),
  last1 = window_value("last_value", 0, 999),
  last2 = window_value("last_value", 1000, 1999),
  last3 = window_value("last_value", 2000, 2999)),
  outputs = omop_output("wide", rows = "entry", format = "wide"))
recipe_execute(windows, out = c(wide = "D_windows"), datasources = conns)

No eligible nonmissing value gives NA. It never gives zero hemoglobin. Before analysing a period, count its missing values and summarise its first and last readings. The following loop repeats the same three explicit aggregate calls.

window_results <- lapply(1:3, function(period) {
  first_name <- paste0("D_windows$first", period)
  last_name <- paste0("D_windows$last", period)
  first_mean <- dsBaseClient::ds.mean(first_name, type = "combine", datasources = conns)
  last_mean <- dsBaseClient::ds.mean(last_name, type = "combine", datasources = conns)
  data.frame(Period = period,
    First = first_mean$Global.Mean[1, 1], Last = last_mean$Global.Mean[1, 1],
    Observed = first_mean$Global.Mean[1, "Nvalid"], Missing = first_mean$Global.Mean[1, "Nmissing"])
})
do.call(rbind, window_results)
Period First Last Observed Missing
1 13.986 14.286 28 0
2 15.300 15.300 10 18
3 14.567 14.567 15 13

In periods 2 and 3, first equals last (15.30 and 14.57 g/dL): each observed person has only one reading in those windows. In period 1, some have repeated readings. These means use the observed people in each period; changing means can therefore reflect changing membership. A missing measurement does not prove that the person left observation. Check observation coverage separately for a follow-up analysis.

Check. Make missingness a named category for each period and release its counts.

Worked answer

ds.omop.mutate("D_windows",
  missing1 = ifelse(is.na(first1), "missing", "observed"),
  missing2 = ifelse(is.na(first2), "missing", "observed"),
  missing3 = ifelse(is.na(first3), "missing", "observed"),
  newobj = "D_missing", datasources = conns)
dsBaseClient::ds.table("D_missing$missing1",
  datasources = conns)$output.list$TABLES.COMBINED_all.sources_counts
#> D_missing$missing1
#> observed       NA 
#>       28        0
dsBaseClient::ds.table("D_missing$missing2",
  datasources = conns)$output.list$TABLES.COMBINED_all.sources_counts
#> D_missing$missing2
#>  missing observed       NA 
#>       18       10        0
dsBaseClient::ds.table("D_missing$missing3",
  datasources = conns)$output.list$TABLES.COMBINED_all.sources_counts
#> D_missing$missing3
#>  missing observed       NA 
#>       13       15        0

The tables show 28, 10 and 15 observed people: therefore 0, 18 and 13 missing values. Do not carry a measurement forward without declaring how long it remains valid and what that assumption means.

Wide columns at prespecified time points

A wide table can hold several scheduled values for each person. A named grid makes the target times, tolerances and selection rule explicit. Each value comes from an eligible observed event; no measurement is interpolated.

points <- omop_timepoints(list(
  baseline = omop_timepoint(),
  year5 = omop_timepoint(5, "years", tolerance = c(-365, 365))),
  anchor = "index", reuse = FALSE)
repeated_hb <- omop_repeated(lab, values = list(hb = omop_number_rows(lab)),
  timepoints = points, missing = "keep")
repeated_recipe <- omop_recipe(events = list(lab), populations = list(entry),
  variables = list(measurements = repeated_hb),
  outputs = omop_output("wide", rows = "entry", format = "wide"))
repeated_result <- recipe_execute(repeated_recipe, out = "D_timepoints", datasources = conns)
dsBaseClient::ds.colnames("D_timepoints", datasources = conns)
#> $site
#> [1] "row_id"                   "cohort_row_id"            "person_id"               
#> [4] "measurements_hb_baseline" "measurements_hb_year5"

The generated names retain the measurement and time-point names. closest is the default selection; first or last would choose differently within the inclusive tolerance. reuse = FALSE prevents an event from filling two points. The tolerance here is a teaching choice for irregular data, not a claim that a lab a year away represents a clinical five-year visit.

Check. Inspect the five-year column’s released summary and missing count.

Solution: a scheduled column

dsBaseClient::ds.summary(
  "D_timepoints$measurements_hb_year5", datasources = conns)
#> $site
#> $site$class
#> [1] "numeric"
#> 
#> $site$length
#> [1] 28
#> 
#> $site$`quantiles & mean`
#>       5%      10%      25%      50%      75%      90%      95%     Mean 
#> 12.59000 12.88000 13.25000 16.00000 16.75000 17.20000 17.29000 15.15333
dsBaseClient::ds.numNA("D_timepoints$measurements_hb_year5", datasources = conns)
#> $site
#> [1] 13

The five-year point has 15 observed and 13 missing values, with a mean of 15.15 g/dL among those observed. The tolerance is ±365 days; this selects a nearby observation without inventing a scheduled reading.

Check. Where can you check the expanded columns’ types before modelling?

Solution: the published table codebook

recipe_codebook(repeated_result)[[1]]$columns[c("name", "r_type")]
name r_type
row_id character
cohort_row_id character
person_id character
measurements_hb_baseline double
measurements_hb_year5 double

Use the numeric columns in a model only after choosing how to handle missing scheduled readings. A codebook does not expose their missingness frequency.

Ask the recipe, or reshape on the server

The installed ds.reShape() can turn existing wide columns into period rows. The native recipe uses names without dots. Create three private aliases with the first.1, first.2, first.3 names expected by this dsBase reshape method. This operation assigns privately; it never returns individual rows.

for (period in 1:3) {
  dsBaseClient::ds.asNumeric(x.name = paste0("D_windows$first", period),
    newobj = paste0("first.", period), datasources = conns)
}
dsBaseClient::ds.dataFrame(c("D_windows$person_id", "first.1", "first.2", "first.3"),
  newobj = "D_for_reshape", datasources = conns)
#> $is.object.created
#> [1] "A data object <D_for_reshape> has been created in all specified data sources"
#> 
#> $validity.check
#> [1] "<D_for_reshape> appears valid in all sources"
dsBaseClient::ds.reShape("D_for_reshape", varying = c("first.1", "first.2", "first.3"),
  timevar.name = "period", idvar.name = "person_id", direction = "long",
  newobj = "D_reshaped", datasources = conns)
#> $is.object.created
#> [1] "A data object <D_reshaped> has been created in all specified data sources"
#> 
#> $validity.check
#> [1] "<D_reshaped> appears valid in all sources"
dsBaseClient::ds.colnames("D_reshaped", datasources = conns)
#> $site
#> [1] "person_id" "period"    "first"

This gives each person three period rows, including missing first values. Only the person key and three first values enter this reshape; last values are not copied into every period. Its period is 1, 2 or 3, not an actual measurement date. A reshape cannot recover dates or readings discarded by a reducer. ds.reShape also depends on the server’s allowed privacy profile; our server allows it.

For a dense panel with last values and event counts, ask the recipe directly. The native panel supports last and mean, but not a first analysis. The wide window reducers above provide first values explicitly without inventing a panel option.

panel <- omop_recipe(events = list(lab), populations = list(entry),
  outputs = omop_output("panel", rows = "entry", format = "person_period",
    options = list(sources = list(lab), bins = list(width = 1000L),
      window = omop_window(0, 2999), analyses = c("count", "last"), representation = "dense")))
recipe_execute(panel, out = c(panel = "D_panel"), datasources = conns)
dsBaseClient::ds.colnames("D_panel", datasources = conns)
#> $site
#> [1] "row_id"            "cohort_row_id"     "person_id"         "period_start_days"
#> [5] "period_end_days"   "days"              "hb_count"          "hb_last"

The panel respects observation coverage and retains empty observed bins: a zero count and a missing last value describe different things. It can omit time outside coverage, so it need not have the same roster as the wide-window reshape. Requesting the right shape keeps keys, windows, coverage and event semantics in one checked plan.

Exercise 1. Verify that the reshape kept three rows per person, without reading rows.

Worked answer

period_counts <- dsBaseClient::ds.table("D_reshaped$period", datasources = conns)
period_counts$output.list$TABLES.COMBINED_all.sources_counts
#> D_reshaped$period
#>  1  2  3 NA 
#> 28 28 28  0

There are 28 rows in each period, including rows with missing measurements. That is 84 rows, still 28 people. A row-count increase is not a sample-size increase.

Build a risk set for a discrete-time hazard

A hazard is the probability of an outcome in the current period among people still at risk at its start. Here the outcome is the next recorded hemoglobin, not illness or death. Start on day 1 after the first reading, and stop at the first subsequent reading, death, observation end or day 7300, whichever comes first. The absence of a repeat lab is not a normal result.

For this section use the same two Synthea sites as chapter 14: 14 different people at each. No people are duplicated; a real multisite study must establish nonoverlapping populations separately. As there, the second connection uses the handle pair, and the earlier conns connection stays available for the later single-site exercises.

two_conns <- ds.omop.login(rep("https://localhost:8443", 2), user = "administrator",
  password = "password",
  server = c("north", "south"),
  resource = c(north = "omop.synthea_north", south = "omop.synthea_south"),
  symbol = "pair")$conns

The panel already stops at observation coverage. Attach one first-outcome day and one death day per episode, using a checked many-to-one join. These dates are index-relative numbers and stay private.

death <- omop_event("death", name = "death")
hazard <- omop_recipe(events = list(lab, death), populations = list(entry), variables = list(
  next_day = omop_variable(event = lab,
    reducer = omop_reduce("first_date", window = omop_window(1, NULL))),
  death_day = omop_variable(event = death, reducer = omop_reduce("first_date"))),
  outputs = list(
    omop_output("daily", rows = "entry", format = "person_period",
      options = list(sources = list(lab), bins = list(width = 1L),
        window = omop_window(1, 7300), analyses = "count", representation = "dense")),
    omop_output("ends", rows = "entry", format = "wide"),
    omop_output("risk", rows = "entry", format = "joined",
      options = list(from = list(list(output = "daily"), list(output = "ends")),
        how = "left", cardinality = "many_to_one"))), publish = "risk")
recipe_execute(hazard, out = c(risk = "D_days"), datasources = two_conns, symbol = "pair")

Remove days after the first repeat or death. A missing next-day value means “no subsequent lab found”, so retain observed days until another censor applies. We count an event on the death day if both dates coincide; state this tie rule.

ds.omop.mutate("D_days", to_next = next_day - period_start_days,
  to_death = death_day - period_start_days,
  newobj = "D_remaining", datasources = two_conns, symbol = "pair")
ds.omop.filter("D_remaining",
  expr = omop_where((is.na(to_next) | to_next >= 0) &
  (is.na(to_death) | to_death >= 0)),
  newobj = "D_risk", datasources = two_conns, symbol = "pair")
ds.omop.mutate("D_risk", event = ifelse(hb_count > 0, 1L, 0L),
  years = period_start_days / 365.25,
  newobj = "D_hazard", datasources = two_conns, symbol = "pair")
hazard_counts <- dsBaseClient::ds.table("D_hazard$event", datasources = two_conns)
hazard_counts$output.list$TABLES.COMBINED_all.sources_counts
#> D_hazard$event
#>     0     1    NA 
#> 48535    25     0

Each row is one observed day at risk. More than one lab on that day is still one outcome. Time in years is a predictor; the outcome probability remains per day. The binomial GLM models log odds with a linear time trend. A study would assess that time specification and the assumption of noninformative censoring.

hazard_fit <- dsBaseClient::ds.glm("event ~ years", data = "D_hazard",
  family = "binomial", datasources = two_conns)
hazard_table <- as.data.frame(hazard_fit$coefficients[, 1:4, drop = FALSE])
hazard_table[["p-value"]] <- format.pval(hazard_table[["p-value"]], digits = 3, eps = 1e-16)
hazard_table
Estimate Std. Error z-value p-value
(Intercept) -12.9553 1.2056 -10.7463 < 1e-16
years 1.2945 0.2344 5.5221 3.35e-08

The event table has 25 first repeats among 28 people. The positive time coefficient means a repeat becomes more likely on a given day among those still without a repeat, under the assumed linear log-odds trend.

This is a jointly estimated distributed GLM. Its risk-set likelihood has one first event at most per person; it is not a logistic model of every recurrent reading treated as an independent patient.

Exercise 2. Show the fitted odds ratio per additional year since entry. Does it mean a yearly probability of getting a lab?

Worked answer

b <- hazard_fit$coefficients["years", 1]
se <- hazard_fit$coefficients["years", 2]
data.frame(Daily_odds_ratio = exp(b), Lower_95 = exp(b - 1.96 * se),
  Upper_95 = exp(b + 1.96 * se))
Daily_odds_ratio Lower_95 Upper_95
3.649 2.305 5.777

The daily odds ratio is 3.65 (95% CI 2.31–5.78) per additional year since entry. It compares the odds of a repeat on the current day, conditional on having remained at risk, for a one-year difference in time since entry. It is not a causal effect or an annual risk. The event is recorded care, not disease onset.

Repeated measures and mixed models

Use the measured BMI concept and kg/m² unit found, inspected and saved in chapter 4’s measured BMI discovery. The measurement is Body mass index 3038553, with unit 9531, kg/m². For actual repeated-value modelling use Synthea’s BMI readings, whose within-person trajectories provide a more useful random-intercept example than hemoglobin here. A random intercept lets people have different baseline levels and accounts for correlation between their repeated readings. This is a different question from time to the first repeat lab.

bmi <- omop_event("measurement", concepts = 3038553L, value = "value_as_number",
  unit = omop_unit(9531L), name = "bmi")
bmi_entry <- omop_population("bmi_entry", index = omop_index(bmi))
repeated <- omop_recipe(events = list(bmi), populations = list(bmi_entry),
  outputs = omop_output("long", rows = "bmi_entry", format = "long", sources = "bmi",
    options = list(columns_derived = c("value", "unit", "days_since_previous"))))
recipe_execute(repeated, out = c(long = "D_long"), datasources = two_conns, symbol = "pair")
dsBaseClient::ds.colnames("D_long", datasources = two_conns)
#> $north
#>  [1] "row_id"                      "cohort_row_id"              
#>  [3] "person_id"                   "concept_id"                 
#>  [5] "start_date"                  "end_date"                   
#>  [7] "measurement_type_concept_id" "value_as_concept_id"        
#>  [9] "meas_event_field_concept_id" "days_since_previous"        
#> [11] "value"                       "unit_concept_id"            
#> 
#> $south
#>  [1] "row_id"                      "cohort_row_id"              
#>  [3] "person_id"                   "concept_id"                 
#>  [5] "start_date"                  "end_date"                   
#>  [7] "measurement_type_concept_id" "value_as_concept_id"        
#>  [9] "meas_event_field_concept_id" "days_since_previous"        
#> [11] "value"                       "unit_concept_id"

start_date is days since first BMI under the default relative-date policy. The person key, all readings and their dates stay on the servers. Preserve actual time; coding visit numbers as equally spaced would misrepresent these records. Each person has exactly one indexed episode here, so cohort_row_id is the person-level grouping key for these models. With multiple episodes per person, use person_id to group repeated observations of the same person; cohort_row_id identifies an episode.

ds.omop.mutate("D_long", years = start_date / 365.25,
  above_cutoff = ifelse(value >= 25, 1L, 0L),
  newobj = "D_repeat", datasources = two_conns, symbol = "pair")
repeat_groups <- dsBaseClient::ds.meanSdGp("D_repeat$value", "D_repeat$above_cutoff",
  type = "combine", datasources = two_conns)
data.frame(Band = c("below 25", "25 or above"),
  Readings = as.numeric(repeat_groups$Nvalid_gp),
  Mean_BMI = as.numeric(repeat_groups$Mean_gp))
Band Readings Mean_BMI
below 25 123 19.130
25 or above 315 28.362

The 438 readings split into 123 below and 315 at or above 25. Each mean’s denominator is the number of readings in that band, not the number of people. People with more readings contribute more to these means. The cutoff is a teaching rule only: this synthetic population includes children, and an adult BMI cutoff is not an age-specific clinical classification. The continuous and binary responses answer different questions.

SLMA means study-level meta-analysis. Each server fits its own mixed model; only estimates and standard errors return for pooling. It is not a single mixed model fitted jointly to concatenated rows. A fixed-effect pool assumes a common coefficient. A random-effects pool allows site coefficients to differ; here use REML to estimate their between-site variance. With only two sites, that variance and the pooled interval remain uncertain.

Optimizer convergence alone does not establish that the data support a model; the binary example below illustrates this.

linear_mixed <- dsBaseClient::ds.lmerSLMA("value ~ years + (1|cohort_row_id)",
  dataName = "D_repeat", datasources = two_conns)
site_slopes <- data.frame(Site = names(two_conns),
  Estimate = as.numeric(linear_mixed$betamatrix.all["years", ]),
  SE = as.numeric(linear_mixed$sematrix.all["years", ]))
site_slopes
Site Estimate SE
north 0.2008 0.0211
south 0.0938 0.0224 
pooled <- linear_mixed$SLMA.pooled.ests.matrix
pooled[, c("pooled.FE", "se.FE", "pooled.REML", "se.REML"), drop = FALSE]
pooled.FE se.FE pooled.REML se.REML
(Intercept) 23.3505 0.9636 23.3462 1.3860
years 0.1507 0.0154 0.1476 0.0535

The site slopes are about 0.201 and 0.094 BMI units per year. They differ strongly (I² about 92%); a common-effect standard error understates this disagreement. The REML standard error is about 3.5 times the fixed-effect one. Interpret the random-effects estimate and interval, while remembering that two sites provide little information about the distribution of site effects. Growth may also be nonlinear, so this straight-line model is only a demonstration.

b <- pooled["years", "pooled.REML"]
se <- pooled["years", "se.REML"]
data.frame(BMI_units_per_year = b, Lower_95 = b - 1.96 * se,
  Upper_95 = b + 1.96 * se)
BMI_units_per_year Lower_95 Upper_95
0.148 0.043 0.252

The average slope is 0.148 BMI units per year (95% normal interval 0.043–0.252). The interval expresses uncertainty about the average site slope under the random-effects model. It is not the range of individual people’s slopes.

A binary model the data do not support well

Turning BMI into a ≥25 flag changes the question and discards information. In the public synthetic records, 19 of 27 measured people stay on one side of this cutoff throughout follow-up. The cutoff is a teaching choice, not a clinical classification for this population, which includes children.

binary_mixed <- dsBaseClient::ds.glmerSLMA("above_cutoff ~ years + (1|cohort_row_id)",
  family = "binomial", dataName = "D_repeat", datasources = two_conns)
binary_sites <- data.frame(Site = names(two_conns),
  Intercept = as.numeric(binary_mixed$betamatrix.all["(Intercept)", ]),
  Time_coefficient = as.numeric(binary_mixed$betamatrix.all["years", ]),
  Random_intercept_SD = vapply(binary_mixed$output.summary[c("study1", "study2")],
    function(x) as.data.frame(x$varcor)$sdcor[1], numeric(1)))
binary_sites
Site Intercept Time_coefficient Random_intercept_SD
north -9.38 1.28 17.32
south 9.25 0.00 12.43

Site intercepts near −9.4 and +9.2 and random-intercept standard deviations near 17 and 12 logits indicate extreme separation between people. Even an optimizer that reports convergence does not make these data informative for this model. We do not interpret a pooled binary effect here.

Exercise 3. Would changing the pooling method repair this binary model?

Solution: assess support before pooling

No. The extreme site estimates arise before pooling. Inspect within-person outcome variation and site variance components; use the continuous response if it answers the question, or reconsider the study design. A different pooling method cannot create missing information.

Recap

Choose the row meaning first. Keep actual time for irregular readings; distinguish missing values, absent events and time outside observation. Request the recipe’s shape when possible, and understand what information a reshape cannot recover. A first-event hazard needs an at-risk panel with follow-up stopped at the event. Repeated-measure models instead retain repeated readings and model their dependence. Check every site’s diagnostics and distinguish joint GLM estimation from SLMA pooling.
